items.text: Reconstructing institutional population denominators and distinguishing differences in entry into institutions from differences in being recommended for sterilization within institutions adds comparable group evidence to the historical narrative.

Nine institutions over thirty-plus years and 212 variables support analysis of differences across time, institutions, and diagnostic categories, providing more granular understanding than merely repeating the known existence of discrimination.

Combining group patterns with close reading of texts on refusal, resistance, and coerced consent preserves the agency of those recorded and constitutes an ELSI and public history contribution; the archive development is a separately supported companion effort.

Recommendation records do not equal performed surgeries; ten-year recommendation flows versus single-time-point population stocks, repeat residents/recommendations, and annual variations affect denominators and risk interpretation, and the case-cohort label does not automatically resolve this.

Hispanic surnames are only an ethnic proxy; cross-era classification, spelling variations, missing data, and institutional diagnostic recording biases must be addressed, and official allegations should not be treated as objective behavioral facts.

Surviving protest letters and explicit refusals select for those who could express themselves and left records; silence/signatures cannot simply be treated as voluntary or non-resistant, and the interpretation of qualitative coding and quantitative associations must retain this point.
